sentences.text: The genus name Cruralispennia translates to "shin feather," while the species name multidonta means "many-toothed."
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a semi-articulated partial skeleton surrounded by carbonized feathers.
The left lower jaw preserves fourteen teeth, a notably high number for enantiornitheans.
Its pygostyle is short and broad, tapering into an upturned tip.
Cruralispennia possessed a short forelimb featuring a robust humerus typical of enantiornitheans.
Sharp, curved claws adorned the toes of this bird.
The unique wire-like leg feathers, known as PWFDT, are currently known only in Cruralispennia.
The early appearance of this derived genus suggests the evolutionary history of ornithothoraces is older than previously indicated by fossils.
Evidence suggests that individuals of Cruralispennia grew rapidly, reaching adult size in less than one year.
The genus Cruralispennia was formally described by Wang and colleagues in 2017.
The only known specimen was found in the Huajiying Formation in China.
A histological study of the humerus found no lines of arrested growth, indicating the individual died within a single season.
Cruralispennia's rapid growth strategy contrasts with other enantiornithines, which are believed to have taken several years to reach adulthood.
Researchers suggest that the crural PWFDT feathers may have functioned in insulation, heat shielding, or social signaling.
The narrow crural PWFDT feathers were likely too simple for aerodynamic use but narrow enough not to hinder flight.
Cruralispennia is classified within Enantiornithes based on humerus features, lack of procoracoid processes, and a long scapular acromion.
The genus Cruralispennia lived during the Hauterivian stage, from 132.6 to 125.77 million years ago.
It is debated whether the unique leg feathers are a novel type or simply immature feathers formed after a recent molt.
